item.title: Gold heads for steep weekly loss as oil prices fuel Fed rate concerns
item.description: Gold eased on Friday, headed for its steepest weekly decline in over four months as elevated oil prices bolstered higher-for-longer interest rate expectations, while investors awaited next week's Federal Reserve policy meeting.
item.dc:creator: Sukanya Mitra
item.content:encoded: Gold eased on Friday, headed for its steepest weekly decline in over four months as elevated oil prices bolstered higher-for-longer interest rate expectations, while investors awaited next week's Federal Reserve policy meeting. Spot gold eased 0.1% to $4,021.04 per ounce by 0554 GMT, paring losses slightly after touching its lowest level since July 20 earlier in the session. The metal has fallen 3.6% so far this week, putting it on track for its worst week since June. US gold futures for December delivery dropped 0.6% to $4,035.50. Speculators are trying to defend the key $4,000 level for gold because a clean break below would signal that the market has stopped pricing rate relief and started pricing sticky inflation, elevated yields, and a stronger dollar, said Monte Safieddine, head of market research at Capital.com. Oil prices [USN:L1N46903W TEXT:"rose"] on Friday after [USN:L1N46809Q TEXT:"Houthi attacks"] in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East. Elevated energy prices bolster expectations of higher-for-longer interest rates by the Fed, increasing the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion. "Any further escalation on the geopolitical front risks pushing oil even higher. Higher oil is reviving inflation fears, lifting yields, and delaying Fed easing. That is a difficult cocktail for bullion," Safieddine added. Focus has turned to the Fed's October 27-28 policy meeting and next week's Personal Consumption Expenditures data, a closely watched gauge because it is the central bank's preferred inflation measure for its 2% inflation target. Traders are largely expecting the central bank to leave interest rates unchanged next week, but expectations for an interest rate hike in December remain at 76%. Meanwhile, analysts at HSBC [USN:L1N46811L TEXT:"cut their average"] 2026 platinum and palladium price forecasts in a research note on Thursday, citing shifting market fundamentals and investor liquidation. Among other metals, spot silver slid 0.4% to $54.31 per ounce, platinum rose 0.3% to $1,574.33 and palladium gained 0.3% to $1,056.49. However, all three metals were headed for weekly declines.

item.title: Asian Football Confederation boss says governing body is backing Infantino
item.description: Asian Football Confederation head Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa said on Friday the regional body would support Gianni Infantino's bid for reelection as FIFA president.
item.dc:creator: Irene Wang
item.content:encoded: Asian Football Confederation head Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa said on Friday the regional body would support Gianni Infantino's bid for reelection as FIFA president. Sheikh Salman had previously backed opposition to Infantino's failed plan to sell off the commercial rights to FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup, to private investors. He had joined with the presidents of UEFA and CONCACAF to pen an open letter calling the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan formulated by Infantino a "fundamental breach of trust". Infantino has apologised for mistakes "in relation to the communication and consultation process" for the FFE. In Sheikh Salman's opening remarks at the AFC's extraordinary congress in Tokyo, the Bahraini said the region supported Infantino. "I think that we reaffirm our full commitment, of course, to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as a FIFA president," he said in comments directed at the Swiss-Italian, who was present at the meeting. Infantino is up for reelection in March as he seeks a fourth term until 2031. Potential candidates must submit their nominations by November 18. IN THE PAST Several key AFC members, including Saudi Arabia and Qatar, had publicly declared their support for Infantino, and while Sheikh Salman acknowledged he had not seen eye to eye with the FIFA president on certain issues he said it was important to look to the future. "I want to make it clear: yes, we had some issues we spoke about in the past but let's not relate the two things together," said Sheikh Salman, who is also seeking a fourth term in office next year. "I think the last few days we met in Zurich. You made it clear that there was a true, a clear understanding between us. "We need to move forward. And we believe football is strongest when we work together with a shared vision and a common purpose. "As one Asian family we are ready to move forward, united in your support Gianni. I just want to make that clear today." Infantino also gave Sheikh Salman his backing in his address to delegates. "You've been doing a fantastic job in AFC in the last 13 years, my dear Salman," he said. "You will do fantastically as well for the next how many years you want. And always, always with my full support, with the partnership of FIFA, because we have seen what we have been doing in the last years." Asked later about Sheikh Salman's comments, Infantino said: "I feel great about the AFC's support." While Africa has also backed Infantino's reelection, he continues to face opposition from European soccer's governing body. UEFA has sent a [USN:L4N466094 TEXT:"letter"] to FIFA seeking answers about his presidency, including questions over the FFE project and the FIFA Peace Prize. Reuters has contacted UEFA for a response to the AFC president's comments at the extraordinary congress.

item.title: Rupee weakens on risk-off sentiment from oil prices, global AI jitters
item.description: The Indian rupee weakened on Friday as soaring oil prices and AI-related jitters fuelled risk aversion, outweighing relief from a pullback in expectations of Federal Reserve rate hikes.
item.dc:creator: Nimesh Vora
item.content:encoded: The Indian rupee weakened on Friday as soaring oil prices and AI-related jitters fuelled risk aversion, outweighing relief from a pullback in expectations of Federal Reserve rate hikes. The rupee was at 94.96 to the US dollar, down from 94.8175 on Thursday. Investors have been reassessing technology valuations and pulling back from riskier assets on worries about stretched AI valuations, leading the markets to sharply pare expectations of Federal Reserve rate hike next week to less than 10% from 70% a month ago. While this has weighed on the dollar and Treasury yields, offering some support to the rupee, rising crude prices have outweighed the relief by fuelling concerns about inflation and imported energy costs. Brent crude surged to its highest since May 4 on Thursday after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia heightened concerns over the security of regional oil infrastructure and shipping routes. Prices remained on the upswing in Asian trade on Friday, with the prospect of further supply disruptions keeping the market anxious. Brent was last hovering near $114 a barrel. For the rupee, the key question is whether a softer dollar can offset the drag from oil and deteriorating risk sentiment, a currency trader at a bank said. "The currency's recovery faces a key test with high crude prices colliding with a broader de-risking impulse," he said. The rupee is also navigating IPO-related flows, with bankers pointing to some residual activity linked to the Jio Platforms offering. These flows, alongside the unwinding of dollar-long positions, had lifted the currency to a six-week high of 94.30 per dollar on Thursday, before oil-related pressure prompted importers to step up dollar purchases.

item.title: Oil spill from tanker hits Umm Al Quwain coast, beaches shut
item.description: An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the coast of Umm Al Quwain, prompting containment operations and environmental assessments, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the coast of Umm Al Quwain, prompting containment operations and environmental assessments, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday. The ministry said all beaches and coastal areas in Umm Al Quwain had been temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures. The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions. The announcement followed reports of a strange odour by residents in some emirates on social media. The ministry said that odours reported by residents in Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain posed no health risks to them. The ministry did not say what caused the spill, and authorities have not identified the tanker involved. The spill adds to heightened concern over maritime security in Gulf waters after a series of attacks on commercial vessels, including incidents outside the Strait of Hormuz. On October 9, a vessel, identified by shipping sources as GEM No.2, was [USN:L1N45V0GU TEXT:"struck "]by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the UAE, causing a fire that was later extinguished. While no group claimed responsibility, maritime security sources told Reuters the incident occurred outside the Strait of Hormuz and pointed to a widening of risks for commercial shipping. Earlier that week, a tanker was also struck off the coast of Qatar inside the Gulf. The spill also follows a [USN:L8N4490KK TEXT:"separate "]tanker-related environmental incident in the region. In August, oil from a tanker that ran aground off Oman began reaching the mainland coast, prompting concerns about environmental damage and cleanup efforts.

item.title: Brandt Clarke lifts Kings past Islanders in overtime
item.description: Brandt Clarke scored with 2:17 left in overtime for the Los Angeles Kings, who edged the New York Islanders 3-2 on Thursday in Elmont, N.Y.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Brandt Clarke scored with 2:17 left in overtime for the Los Angeles Kings, who edged the New York Islanders 3-2 on Thursday in Elmont, N.Y. The Kings controlled play for much of overtime before Clarke beat screened goaltender Semyon Varlamov with a shot over his shoulder. Artemi Panarin scored twice in the first period for the Kings, who have won two straight since opening the season 0-4-2. Goalie Darcy Kuemper made 41 saves and assisted on the winning goal. Clarke also registered an assist. Victor Eklund and Matthew Schaefer scored for the Islanders, who extended their point streak to five games (3-0-2). Varlamov, seeking his first win since Nov. 14, 2024, recorded 24 saves, including a stop on Adrian Kempe's second-period penalty shot. The goalie missed last season after undergoing double partial knee replacements. The Kings were outshot 15-6 in the first period but took a 2-0 lead thanks to Panarin's goals. Los Angeles nearly turned the puck over before Panarin opened the scoring at 5:51. Alex Laferriere couldn't corral a pass from Clarke in the neutral zone, but Clarke shoved it back to Laferriere before the right winger dished it to Panarin. The former New York Rangers star eluded Logan Stanley, then waited for Schaefer to drop to one knee before firing a shot from the right faceoff circle over Varlamov's glove. Panarin scored an unassisted goal to double the lead with 3:23 remaining when his first shot glanced off Bo Horvat, and he buried the rebound as Varlamov was surrounded by teammates. Varlamov kept the score at 2-0 by stopping Kempe with 9:01 left before Eklund began the Islanders' comeback bid by scoring on the power play less than four minutes later. Eklund and Tony DeAngelo exchanged passes at the top of the slot before Eklund, stationed above the left faceoff circle, fired a shot under Kuemper's glove with 5:54 remaining. Schaefer tied the score with his first goal of the season 7:06 into the third, when he took a pass from Stanley, moved into the middle of the right faceoff circle and beat Kuemper stick side. --Field Level Media

item.title: Data centres fail as AI pick-and-shovel trade
item.description: NextDC shares fell 42% after community backlash delayed power upgrades at one site. Investors are wising up to the trade-offs of massive debt-financed spending, slow-moving utilities, chip shortages and impatient hyperscaler clients like OpenAI with ironclad get-out clauses.
item.dc:creator: Antony Currie
item.content:encoded: So much for a safe bet on the AI revolution. The smart advice for investing in potential bubbles is to find the modern equivalent of the picks and shovels of the US gold rush in the 1800s. For today's artificial intelligence trade, data centre providers were supposed to be one of them: no matter whether hyperscalers like OpenAI and Anthropic or any of the other developers of software succeed or fail, the demand for places to host the hardware needed is too strong to shatter. But the stock price crashes at Australia's NextDC (NXT.AX) and its US neocloud rival CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , and the [USN:L6N45V00W TEXT:"aborted $5.5 billion IPO"] of Firmus Technologies, confirm that investors are realising it's not that simple. Start with the non-financial problems. Data centre developers want to build as fast as possible to meet their hyperscaler clients' voracious demand for compute and inference capacity. Trouble is, that can lead to high expectations, poor planning and dismal community relations, even for players like NextDC, whose shares fell 42% on Wednesday, that have been in operation for decades. Semiconductor shortages continue, for example. And utilities need more than a few months to get water and electricity hooked up - one water provider told Breakingviews conversations ought to start up to three years before developers buy the land. Nscale in the UK [USN:L6N4650TB TEXT:"lost a contract"] with Microsoft (MSFT.O) after being told power would not be available until 2030. NextDC similarly misread local opposition to its M3 site in Melbourne right across the street from a residential neighbourhood: the resulting delays to installing up to 22-metre-high concrete poles to carry 66,000-volt cables forced CEO Craig Scroggie to slash its EBITDA forecast by a third, cease projects with no contracts and consider selling undeveloped sites. Such issues can then cascade. Constructing data centres requires lots of investment. That's mostly done with debt, usually raised only once a contract has been signed. While that sounds smart, it leaves the borrower at the mercy of iron-clad get-out clauses. One is the availability clause: if water or power connections are delayed by a stipulated timeframe, if a natural disaster strikes or if chips are either unavailable or subpar, then the hyperscaler client can walk. There's also a more general delay clause, which usually stipulates the customer can cancel the entire contract if completion of the data centre is more than 12 months late. It's bad news for traditional data centre builders and neoclouds alike. They could be left with the unenviable mix of part-finished projects, unused land, underwhelming or no earnings and heaps of debt. Hardly a picks-and-shovels trade. Follow Antony Currie on Bluesky and LinkedIn . Shares in NextDC closed down 42% on October 21 after the Australian data centre builder and operator cut its underlying EBITDA forecast for the financial year to the end of June by more than a third. The company now expects EBITDA of A$245 million to A$265 million ($172 million to $186 million) for the period. CEO Craig Scroggie also said he is putting on hold all projects not already backed by customer contracts, has started a "detailed review" of the company's capital expenditure programme and is open to selling development sites that "are not required in the near term". The move came after Jemena Electricity Networks informed NextDC that it has suspended some of the work to increase power supply to its M3 data centre in Melbourne following "community and stakeholder opposition". Last month local residents used their vehicles and other methods to prevent Jemena from installing concrete electricity poles of up to 22-metres in height that are needed to carry the 66,000-volt power lines the data centre will require. Scroggie also noted that the company had some A$8.7 billion of liquidity at the end of September. Meanwhile, on October 20, after local opposition Amazon abandoned plans to build four data centres on a site it had bought from George Washington University in Virginia in the US. The company also agreed to donate $5 million to the county's housing trust fund. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: 76ers rally from 29 down to stun Cavaliers
item.description: PHILADELPHIA -- Tyrese Maxey scored 32 points as the Philadelphia 76ers erased a 29-point deficit in a wild 114-106 victory over the visiting Cleveland Cavaliers on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: PHILADELPHIA -- Tyrese Maxey scored 32 points as the Philadelphia 76ers erased a 29-point deficit in a wild 114-106 victory over the visiting Cleveland Cavaliers on Thursday. Joel Embiid added 24 points for Philadelphia, which dominated the second half for the second straight game after opening the season Tuesday with a road victory over the New York Knicks. This rally was even more emphatic, as the Sixers outscored the Cavaliers 69-37 after halftime. Playing in front of the home crowd for the first time as 76ers, LeBron James scored 17 points and grabbed 10 rebounds, while Jaylen Brown scored 10 of his 21 points in the fourth quarter. The result was the largest comeback by the 76ers in the play-by-play era (since 1996-97). Cleveland fell short in its season opener despite Donovan Mitchell's 32 points and 10 rebounds. Evan Mobley added 18 points for the Cavaliers, while James Harden had 16 and Jarrett Allen notched 14. After trailing by 24 at halftime, Philadelphia needed only 78 seconds to cut the deficit to 13, as James found Embiid for a layup to make it 69-56. Maxey's layup with 5:42 left in the third quarter brought the Sixers back within 10. Philadelphia got as close as 84-82 before Mario Hezonja made two late bank shots, helping the Cavaliers carry a 90-82 lead into the fourth. Embiid made a running floater with 7:24 left to draw the Sixers within 95-94. He knocked down a 15-footer on the next trip to give the hosts their first lead of the night. Brown scored the next six points and Maxey added a bucket to cap a 15-0 push, giving the Sixers a 104-95 lead. Cleveland got within 106-102 down the stretch, but Mitchell missed two free throws, and the momentum was squashed. Maxey and Brown scored on the next two trips to push the lead back to eight. The Cavaliers stormed out of the gates, taking a 35-18 lead after 12 lopsided minutes. The Sixers shot 38.1% in the first quarter and committed nine turnovers. Philadelphia committed six more turnovers in the second quarter en route to a 69-45 deficit at intermission. Mobley scored 11 second-quarter points and Mitchell had 10 for Cleveland, which led by as many as 29 points in the period. Mitchell paced all scorers with 22 points at the break. --Field Level Media

item.title: Yaroslav Askarov makes career-high 41 saves in Sharks’ win over Senators
item.description: Yaroslav Askarov set a career high with 41 saves for the San Jose Sharks, who won their second straight game by taming the host Ottawa Senators 6-2 on Thursday night.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Yaroslav Askarov set a career high with 41 saves for the San Jose Sharks, who won their second straight game by taming the host Ottawa Senators 6-2 on Thursday night. Collin Graf and Jacob Trouba both finished with a goal and an assist for the Sharks, who won in regulation for the first time this season. Tyler Toffoli and Nolan Allan also lit the lamp, while Zack Ostapchuk and Ivar Stenberg tallied empty-netters in the final 3:29 to secure the victory. Kiefer Sherwood assisted on a pair of goals. Askarov won for the first time since Oct. 3. His previous career high in saves was 39, which he set in a 3-2 overtime loss against Edmonton in December 2024. Tim Stutzle recorded his team-best seventh goal for the Senators, and Jordan Spence got his first of the season. Drake Batherson, Warren Foegele, Fabian Zetterlund and Nikolas Matinpalo set up their Ottawa teammates with assists. Senators goalie Samuel Ersson stopped 22 of the 26 shots he faced. The Sharks broke open a 1-1 game by scoring three goals in a span of 4:05 midway through the second period. Toffoli notched his fourth of the season on a power play with 10:47 left. He scored through traffic from the point after exchanging passes with Sherwood. Trouba got the secondary assist. Graf made it 3-1 on a short-handed goal with eight minutes remaining, and Trouba added his goal 78 seconds later, set up by Graf and Darnell Nurse, who was leaving the penalty box when he received the puck. The Senators, coming off an emotional win over the Florida Panthers, recorded the last 12 shots on goal in the second, but Askarov was up to the task each time. That included a lunging glove save from behind his back to keep Batherson from scoring on what was an open net. The posts were also unkind to the Senators. Carter Yakemchuk had a first-period shot that was initially ruled a goal overturned after replay showed it hit the crossbar and a post. Claude Giroux also found the post twice. Stutzle scored on a delayed penalty to give Ottawa the 1-0 lead with 13:44 left in the opening period, but Allan tied it less than five minutes later. Ottawa outshot San Jose 17-6 in the final period. Spence made it 4-2 with 13:36 to go. Ersson was pulled with 3:55 remaining after San Jose's Macklin Celebrini was called for tripping, and the Sharks ultimately added to their lead with the net empty. --Field Level Media

item.title: Yen set for weekly gain as AI jitters spur safe-haven rush
item.description: The Japanese yen was set for its biggest weekly gain since early September, buoyed by safe-haven flows as risk-aversion took hold in the broader markets that pushed US Treasury yields sharply lower and left the dollar hugging a three-week trough.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Japanese yen was set for its biggest weekly gain since early September, buoyed by safe-haven flows as risk-aversion took hold in the broader markets that pushed US Treasury yields sharply lower and left the dollar hugging a three-week trough. The moves in the currency markets were driven by doubts over the AI spending boom even as Brent crude futures stay above $110 per barrel, suggesting concerns over economic growth outweighed inflation worries. The yen firmed as much as 0.4% on Friday to 156.08 per dollar, its strongest level in more than a month, before reversing the gains to 156.89 by midday. It was set for a 0.7% gain for the week. "The yen was bought as a hedge, not as an allocation," said Shoki Omori, chief fixed income strategist for Japan at Deutsche Bank. "But we see no evidence of Japanese institutions repatriating, and the carry against the dollar is intact," he said, adding that the bank expects USD/JPY to trade in a 155-159 range into the Bank of Japan's policy meeting. Data on Friday showed Japan's annual core consumer inflation [USN:L4N46724Q TEXT:"exceeded"] the central bank's 2% target in September for the first time in nine months, a sign of broadening price pressure that bolsters the case for a near-term rate hike. The majority of economists [USN:L4N4650G0 TEXT:"polled"] by Reuters expect a hold on Friday of next week, followed by a quarter-point hike at the following meeting in December. Beyond the BOJ meeting, investors are also bracing for the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank to announce policy decisions next week. Both are also expected to keep interest rates on hold for October. AI WORRIES The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, edged up at 101.64, after touching its lowest level since the beginning of the month at 101.44 on Thursday. US 10-year Treasury yields hovered near a one-month low at 4.9674%, after [USN:L6N4681A9 TEXT:"tumbling"] on Thursday when equities sold off on renewed concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom, burnishing the safe-haven appeal of sovereign debt. The benchmark yield breached the psychologically important 5% last month and has mostly stayed above that level until this week, and the big move lower in yields has helped pull back rate hike bets for next year. "Whether yields stay below 5% is another question," said ING analysts said, adding they still expect the 10-year yield to snap back above 5% eventually, given inflation, fiscal deficit and AI trends. "The risk-off environment takes pressure off the Fed to hike next week. But even given that, we'd not be loading up on duration here, at least not just yet," the analysts said. Brent futures pushed above $114 per barrel, extending a 4% [USN:L1N46801N TEXT:"climb"] from the previous session after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the region. RISING DEMAND FOR SAFETY While demand for safety is intensifying, the beneficiaries differ depending on the risk, OCBC analysts said. AI jitters favour the yen, Middle East tensions support the Canadian dollar and Norwegian crown due to rising oil prices, while French fiscal stress benefits the Swiss franc, they said, adding that AI had become an increasingly two-way macro risk for the US dollar. The Canadian dollar firmed past C$1.40 against the greenback, to its strongest level in a month. The Swiss franc was steady at 0.8211 per dollar, near its firmest level in a month. China's offshore yuan was little changed at 6.6729 per dollar, hovering near its strongest level in more than four years. The euro was largely flat at $1.121. Worries about France's ability to tackle its huge debt burden have hurt French government bonds and raised concern about other heavily indebted euro-area countries, weighing on the euro. The Australian dollar held steady at $0.7015, while the Kiwi dollar rose 0.2% to $0.5695.

item.title: Tech selloff slows in Asia, oil hits five-month high
item.description: A selloff in global tech shares lost some steam in Asia on Friday, after concerns over the enormous funding needs of AI hammered Wall Street and led to the biggest daily rally in Treasuries in more than three years.
item.dc:creator: Stella Qiu
item.content:encoded: A selloff in global tech shares lost some steam in Asia on Friday, after concerns over the enormous [USN:L6N4681D7 TEXT:"funding needs"] of AI hammered Wall Street and led to the biggest daily rally in Treasuries in more than three years. European bourses also look set for a steady start to trading, with pan-region stock futures little changed. Nasdaq futures were off 0.1%, while S&P 500 futures slipped 0.2%. However, Brent crude added 0.9% to hit a new five-month peak of $114.10 a barrel as fears grow that the conflict in the Middle East could escalate. Brent is set to end the week 3.9% higher after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia [USN:L1N46801N TEXT:"stoked concerns"] of further disruption to energy supplies. Treasuries held onto their overnight gains amid the flight to safety. Markets also sharply pared back bets on further policy tightening from the Federal Reserve, stripping out almost a full quarter-point rate hike for next year amid concerns a bursting AI bubble could derail the data-centre investment boom and hobble the US economy. A December rate rise is no longer fully priced, with the implied probability falling to 85%. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares excluding Japan (.MISX00000PUS) was last flat after earlier falling as much as 0.8% as bargain hunting emerged following the steep selloff. Still it was set for a weekly loss to 2.4%, which would be a fourth straight week in the red. Japan's Nikkei (.N225) dropped 0.5% and was down 4.1% for the week. South Korea's KOSPI (.KS11) managed to eke out a 0.1% gain after shedding 4% earlier in the session. Mainland China's blue-chips found support after hitting the lowest since July 2025, with the CSI300 (.CSI300) up 0.8%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng (.HSI) also rose 0.7% after dropping 3% on Thursday. "It is hard to get too bearish on equities overall just yet, with earnings growth still positive and the hard economic data holding up well," said Diana Mousina, Deputy Chief economist at AMP. "All of this means that the AI trade isn’t necessarily over, but it is changing. It is no longer a case of 'buy everything'." On Wall Street, the Nasdaq slumped more than 2%, with Meta (META.O) shares losing nearly 8% after the [USN:L4N4671S3 TEXT:"Facebook parent"] posted its first cash outflow in more than a decade due to its AI-related expenditures. Meta also announced plans to issue non-voting shares in a two-for-one split to raise capital to spend on the technology. Tesla (TSLA.O) shares fell 3.1% as the electric car maker cut its 2026 [USN:L4N4671SD TEXT:"capital spending plans"]. TREASURIES SHINE As tech stocks tumbled, money flowed into safe-haven US Treasuries, sending yields plunging across the curve overnight. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield slid more than 19 basis points, the biggest drop since March 2023, before steadying at 4.9676% on Friday, back below the closely watched [USN:L8N45E1BK TEXT:"5% level"]. That was also due in part to the [USN:L6N4680JM TEXT:"ongoing sell-off"] in French bonds, whose benchmark yield climbed 6 basis points overnight to 5.0601%, the highest level since 2002. "The US 10yr yield gapped back below 5% with some conviction. We're not convinced it keeps on going," said Padhraic Garvey, ING's regional head of research for the Americas. "We're minded to expect it to snap back above (5%), as we still have inflation/fiscal deficit/AI boom underpinnings to navigate. And we have the US midterm elections approaching as an excuse for trouble. But it will need some degree of calm in the risk space first." The 2-year Treasury yield slumped nearly 19 bps overnight and was last flat at 4.6582%. Government bonds in Asia also rallied. The yield on 10-year Japanese government bonds fell 9 bps to 2.780%, while Australia's 10-year yield dropped 8 bps to 5.178%. In currency markets, the dollar steadied at 156.91 yen on Friday, after slumping 0.9% overnight. The dollar rose 0.2% to 0.8219 Swiss franc , after an overnight fall of 0.5%. Gold failed to catch any safe-haven demand though, and was flat at $4,021.99 an ounce on Friday after a nearly 3% drop overnight.

item.title: US tariff war is fueling Vietnam's coal boom
item.description: A years-long trade war between the United States and China has helped shift manufacturing investment, factory output and export production into Vietnam, driving the Southeast Asian nation's coal-fired electricity generation to record highs.
item.dc:creator: Gavin Maguire
item.content:encoded: A years-long trade war between the United States and China has helped shift manufacturing investment, factory output and export production into Vietnam, driving the Southeast Asian nation's coal-fired electricity generation to record highs. Vietnam's coal plants generated 132.9 terawatt hours (TWh) of electricity during the first nine months of 2026, which is a 15% jump from the same months last year and the highest for that period on record, according to data from Ember. A roughly 12% decline in year-to-date hydro power production due to below-normal rainfall this summer has been a key driver of the greater coal-fired activity, forcing utilities to offset stunted reservoir output with higher coal production. But a larger factor has been the steady swell in Vietnam's export-oriented manufacturing sector, which has grown rapidly within the past decade and lifted the country's total electricity demand by nearly 50% since 2019. In many respects, that manufacturing expansion can be traced back to Washington. US tariffs on Chinese imports since 2018 encouraged manufacturers to diversify production into lower-cost locations, with Vietnam emerging as one of the biggest winners. The shift has helped supercharge Vietnam's factory sector and power demand, but it has also tied an increasing volume of export production destined for the US market to a power system that still relies heavily on coal for electricity generation. AMERICA'S FACTORY FLOOR The switch in production origins shows up clearly in US trade data. In 2018, US imports from China were roughly 10 times larger than imports from Vietnam. This year, monthly imports from the two countries have been nearly level. When US imports from China hit their peak of roughly $539 billion, average monthly US trade flows to China were around $45 billion, data from LSEG shows. During that same year, average US monthly trade flows to Vietnam were around $4 billion. So far in 2026, average monthly US trade flows to China and Vietnam have been around $22.9 billion and $22 billion, respectively. That more than 400% rise in the value of Vietnam's monthly exports to the US helped fuel an economy-wide boom, with Vietnam's gross domestic product (GDP) posting an average annual expansion of 7.4% since 2022, according to the International Monetary Fund. That growth pace was one of the world's fastest during that period, and in turn triggered sustained growth in Vietnam's total electricity consumption, which expanded at an average rate of 6% a year between 2022 and 2025, data from Ember shows. COAL-HEAVY POWER MIX Vietnam's electricity system is heavily reliant on coal, with coal-fired power stations accounting for an average of around 49% of total utility supplies since 2019. By comparison, coal accounts for around a third of electricity generation globally, which means that Vietnam has a substantially more coal-dependent power system than most. However, coal's share of Vietnam's power mix can fluctuate significantly depending on the availability of alternative power sources in any given year. For instance, coal only accounted for 38.5% of the power mix in 2022 thanks to strong hydro production that year as well as a surge in international coal prices, which spurred nearly all cost-sensitive power systems to pare back coal use. So far in 2026, coal's share has averaged nearly 52% of the generation mix due to the lowest hydro production tally since 2023. That coal share is the highest for that period since 2020, and has resulted in a 16% jump in power sector emissions to a record 129 million metric tons of carbon dioxide and equivalent gases so far this year, data from Ember shows. And with the peak hydro production period already passed, additional gains in both coal use and coal emissions are likely, which will help cement 2026 as a record for Vietnam's coal power reliance. Over the longer term, Vietnam does have significant non-coal power capacity under construction, including around 11 gigawatts (GW) of gas-fired power, 1.4 GW of new hydro capacity, and around 1.3 GW of wind capacity, according to Global Energy Monitor. But there are also an additional 2.7 GW of new coal plants being built, with a further 2.6 GW planned after that. That means that, having won a growing share of the US import demand, Vietnam looks set to primarily power that production with coal. That in turn may serve to keep the cost of goods production relatively low, but comes with its own climate price tag that US importers may have to wrestle with as and when their supply chains come under scrutiny. item.title: Oil prices rise more than 1% as supply concerns linger
item.description: Oil prices rose over 1% on Friday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Oil prices rose over 1% on Friday after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns of further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East. Brent crude futures climbed $1.30, or 1.2%, to $114.47 a barrel as of 0639 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose $1.37, or 1.4%, to $100.84. Brent, which settled at its highest since May 4 on Thursday, is set to close higher for a third successive week, while WTI is on track to finish higher for a second straight week. Saudi Aramco (2222.SE) on Thursday [USN:L1N46809Q TEXT:"ordered the evacuation"] of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported, as fighting intensified between the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen-based Houthis. "Markets are increasingly worried about renewed escalation in the Persian Gulf, a scenario that could threaten oil flows that have so far remained remarkably resilient," ING analysts said in a note on Friday. "Re-escalation seems the most likely path. Even if tensions don't re-escalate, the mere possibility is likely to keep a sizeable geopolitical risk premium embedded in prices." Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned Houthis pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea. "The key factors to monitor now are the extent of actual disruption and the time needed to restore operations, as these will ultimately determine how much of a supply risk premium the market is willing to pay," said Linh Tran, an analyst at XS.com. "If attacks persist and delay deliveries, elevated prices will have a firmer foundation." In Libya, an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port has been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields, the head of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Thursday.

item.title: Australian TV reporter recalls 'terrifying' rescue of man from sinking car
item.description: An Australian television reporter who rescued a man from a car as it was engulfed by floodwaters said on Friday it was terrifying to watch someone almost drown but added "there are few better feelings" than saving a person's life.
item.dc:creator: Stefica Bikesh
item.content:encoded: An Australian television reporter who rescued a man from a car as it was engulfed by floodwaters said on Friday it was terrifying to watch someone almost drown but added "there are few better feelings" than saving a person's life. Will Murray, a journalist with public broadcaster the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, was reporting on flooding north of the city of Brisbane in Queensland state on Thursday, when a man drove a four-wheel drive through floodwater. It then stalled and started to sink. "It was terrifying. Like, the thought of watching someone drown was just, you know, I can see why people would sort of freeze up, because it is just horrifying to watch someone in distress like that," Murray told Reuters. Murray and bystander Daniel Hainey swam out to the car and pulled the driver from the vehicle, moments before it was completely submerged. Murray didn't get the survivor's name or number, but said he hoped the man was doing well. "You know, we had a big old hug after we got him out, and that was just one of the best moments of my life, I have to say, just the relief of seeing him safe and well. That was enough for me," Murray said. Emergency services in south-east Queensland responded to hundreds of distress calls on Thursday and Friday after more than 200 mm (7.9 inches) of rain caused flash flooding that closed roads and schools.

item.title: Taiwan shuts down ahead of Typhoon Champi, nearly 1,000 flights cancelled
item.description: Almost all of Taiwan shut down on Friday ahead of the arrival of Typhoon Champi, which is forecast to bring strong winds and torrential rain, and though the storm is weakening it could still make direct landfall on the island.
item.dc:creator: Yimou Lee, Angie Teo, Fabian Hamacher
item.content:encoded: Almost all of Taiwan shut down on Friday ahead of the arrival of Typhoon Champi, which is forecast to bring strong winds and torrential rain, and though the storm is weakening it could still make direct landfall on the island. At one point a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of around 191 kph (119 mph) near its centre, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA). The storm was about 220 km (137 miles) east of Taiwan, the CWA said. The storm's forecast track shows it will pass just off northeastern Taiwan, turn north toward the Chinese coast and eventually move into southern Japan. One person was killed and 171 were injured in Taiwan, where the government said 2,639 people had been evacuated from mountainous areas. Taipower said more than 77,000 homes had lost power, though electricity had already been restored to most. CWA forecaster Liu Pei-teng told Reuters that landfall could not be ruled out if it "stalls, loops, or wobbles from side to side" on approach to Taiwan. "The storm's wind radius is quite large, among the bigger ones in recent years," Liu said. "If the storm slows down, the strong winds will affect Taiwan for longer." Coastal towns received mobile phone alerts warning of gusts exceeding 150 kph (93 mph) and urging residents to seek immediate shelter, while nearly a metre (3 feet) of rain was forecast for northern mountain areas, including around Taipei. In the northeastern county of Yilan, where strong winds and heavy showers were intensifying and the typhoon was forecast to pass close by later on Friday, authorities distributed sandbags and put amphibious vehicles and inflatable rescue boats on standby. "When necessary, the military will come in to help people, including using amphibious vehicles for evacuations or disaster relief," said Lee Ming-chen, head of the port town of Suao, which was badly flooded in previous typhoons. In the northern port city of Keelung, boat owners hurried to secure their vessels. "It's not that severe; I'm just worried that there will be flooding. Keelung has seen a lot of flooding this year," said construction worker Liu Yu-en, 18. HUGE RADIUS Taiwan forecasters said the storm's radius was around 320 km (200 miles), large enough to cover most of Taiwan, and weather experts said its impact could last nearly two days. Taiwan's financial markets (.TWII) , also closed on Friday, while only the Taiwan-controlled Kinmen islands, which sit next to the Chinese coast, will open schools and offices as normal. The transport ministry said all 262 domestic flights were cancelled for Friday, along with 717 international ones. The north-south high-speed rail service was operating as usual. In the capital Taipei there were squally showers, but public transport including the subway was working, albeit with reduced service. Taiwan is generally very well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike in autumn too. The typhoon is forecast to first pass over Japan's westernmost inhabited island, Yonaguni, in Okinawa Prefecture.

item.title: GM cancels deal with new US rare-earth magnet plant, documents say
item.description: General Motors , the biggest customer of a US factory making rare earth magnets for electric vehicles, cancelled its long-term supply deal with the manufacturer, and the two sides are in arbitration, according to regulatory documents and a person with knowledge of the situation.
item.dc:creator: Eric Onstad
item.content:encoded: General Motors (GM.N) , the biggest customer of a US factory making rare earth magnets for electric vehicles, cancelled its long-term supply deal with the manufacturer, and the two sides are in arbitration, according to regulatory documents and a person with knowledge of the situation. The move spotlights the challenges Western firms face in building domestic rare-earths output and cutting their reliance on China, which produces about 90% of global permanent magnets. It also shows how the US auto industry's landscape has changed since Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 and cut federal support for electric vehicles. Germany's Vacuumschmelze, or VAC, signed a [USN:L8N34F3IX TEXT:"long-term deal"] in 2023 with GM to supply permanent magnets for its electric vehicles from a new plant in South Carolina. Energy Fuels (UUUU.A) , which agreed in June to pay $1.9 billion to [USN:L4N42V0QM TEXT:"acquire VAC"], said in US Securities and Exchange Commission documents filed last week that a customer of the plant terminated its supply agreement on July 1, and VAC launched arbitration proceedings against that customer several days later. It did not name the customer, but GM this week reported in an SEC filing that a supplier of a component for EV traction motors "initiated an arbitration against us seeking damages after we terminated a strategic sourcing agreement," without saying why it cancelled the deal. The person familiar with the matter confirmed GM was the customer that cancelled the contract with VAC's US unit, e-VAC Magnetics. GM and Energy Fuels declined to comment on the arbitration because it is confidential. The dispute has not been previously reported and none of the companies involved have issued press releases about the issue. VAC launched its $500-million US magnet plant late last year with a capacity of just under 2,000 metric tons a year, and 90% was set to be sold to GM, with the remainder supplying the US government, VAC CEO Erik Eschen [USN:L5N3UY0MF TEXT:"told Reuters"] in September last year. VAC's US unit said it was seeking damages in arbitration due to wrongful termination. "We have no concerns about VAC’s commercial success and its ability to produce rare earth permanent magnets to customer specifications," Energy Fuels said. However, Energy Fuels told Reuters there may be "potential adjustments to our purchase price of VAC depending on the outcome of the arbitration." GM ROLLS BACK EV SALES GM has been pulling back on sales of EVs, which historically have lost money, following the Trump administration’s withdrawal of incentives and tax breaks meant to benefit the industry. In January, GM took a [USN:L6N3Y915L TEXT:"$6 billion charge"] to unwind some EV investments. When GM and VAC announced the supply deal three years ago, VAC said the plant would support GM for a minimum of 10 years and supply a wide range of models. The dispute first arose in April 2026, according to the SEC documents. Energy Fuels said it was aware of the dispute when it was negotiating the VAC acquisition. Energy Fuels, a producer of uranium for the nuclear power industry, said the takeover would allow it to become one of the world's largest non-Chinese producers of magnets used in the aerospace, defence and renewable energy sectors. VAC supplies magnets to more than 1,000 customers, from facilities in Germany, Malaysia and other countries.

item.title: Apple launches into foldable market as iPhone Duo sales begin
item.description: Sales of Apple's first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, began on Friday, with market watchers betting on whether the device can reinvent the small foldables market in the same way the iPhone did for smartphones.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Soni
item.content:encoded: Sales of Apple's (AAPL.O) first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, began on Friday, with market watchers betting on whether the device can reinvent the small foldables market in the same way the iPhone did for smartphones. The Duo's reception could prove an early test for new CEO John Ternus, the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September. It could also have large implications for a niche category in which rivals such as Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and Huawei Technologies have sold premium offerings for several years. Within minutes of pre-orders opening last Friday, Apple's estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response from customers "nothing short of extraordinary." With the massive demand, Apple capped pre-orders at two handsets per customer and limited sales significantly for walk-in shoppers, resulting in muted crowds unlike the hype that typically accompanied new iPhone releases. In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan, units would be available only for customers who had ordered online In Sydney, the first Apple store to sell the phones on Friday, a queue of customers formed outside before opening at 8 a.m. local time (2100 GMT). Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer, paid A$3,899 ($2,734) for a Duo with 512GB memory. "This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it's so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life's too short," he said. In China, a soft consumer market combined with memory costs pushing prices higher has led to [USN:P8N44H02N TEXT:"six straight quarters"] of declines in smartphone shipments. Apple's market share, however, has rebounded as some phone buyers trade up to premium devices while others seek value at the lower end of the market, putting pressure on mid-range brands. Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi (1810.HK) , but still queued outside a central Shanghai Apple store from 6 a.m. to get his hands on Apple's first foldable. "I've used Apple products for many years and I have more trust (in the brand), so I bought one on launch day to try it out," he said. In Hong Kong, May, 38, who declined to give his full name for privacy reasons, secured a 256GB iPhone Duo, which retails for HK$17,499 ($2,231.73), during an online pre‑sale and aimed to resell the handset for a profit of around HK$4,000: “A few meals' worth of money,” he joked. MIXED REVIEWS Early reviews have praised the Duo's design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers. But reviewers have said camera compromises including the absence of a telephoto lens and third-party apps that still need to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers. They have also said the Duo in its smaller, folded state is less handy for the litany of quick tasks that most users carry out each day on standard iPhones, with several prominent reviewers recommending against the Duo for many Apple customers. "It's been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I've gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I'd want to buy and carry," longtime Apple commentator John Gruber, author of the blog Daring Fireball, wrote in a review. Tech commentator Marques Brownlee, popularly known as MKBHD, said in a YouTube review that "if you're just a regular person who doesn't do much more than texting, social media and browsing here and there, then it is probably a no. But if the $2,000 doesn't mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone." TOUGH TO FIND The limited supplies could disappoint Apple fans lining up in front of stores to buy the Duo. Apple told Reuters that walk-in availability would vary by country, with limited stocks in the US, Australia, Canada, Mexico and much of Britain and Europe. "Foldables have been an established category for years, but adoption has remained relatively limited compared with conventional smartphones. Apple's entry could bring the format to a much broader audience," said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president at market researcher IDC. IDC expects Apple will take 44% of the foldable value in 2026 on 31% of foldable units. By 2027, it will become the market leader in the category both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast. "Apple has made a convincing case for this form factor," Jeronimo said after spending a week with the passport-shaped Duo. "Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market," Jeronimo said. ($1 = 1.4257 Australian dollars) ($1 = 7.8410 Hong Kong dollars)

item.title: Kering-Le recul des ventes de Gucci au T3 pèse sur les espoirs de relance
item.description: Le groupe de luxe français Kering a annoncé jeudi une baisse des ventes de Gucci au troisième trimestre, la faiblesse persistante de la fréquentation de ses magasins compliquant les efforts de redressement engagés par son directeur général Luca de Meo.
item.dc:creator: Tassilo Hummel, Alessandro Parodi, Elena Smirnova
item.content:encoded: Le groupe de luxe français Kering (PRTP.PA) a annoncé jeudi une baisse des ventes de Gucci au troisième trimestre, la faiblesse persistante de la fréquentation de ses magasins compliquant les efforts de redressement engagés par son directeur général Luca de Meo. [USN:L8N40Z0D8 TEXT:"Luca de Meo"], vétéran de l'industrie automobile qui a pris les rênes du groupe l'an dernier, tente de redresser Kering à travers un plan stratégique sur cinq ans visant à doubler sa marge opérationnelle. Mais les tensions au Moyen-Orient, la faiblesse de la demande en Chine et le ralentissement de la dynamique de consommation aux États-Unis compliquent la réalisation de cet objectif. Les ventes trimestrielles inférieures aux attentes publiées récemment par [USN:L8N45Y1DP TEXT:"LVMH"] et [USN:L8N4680BW TEXT:"Hermès"], ainsi que les signes d'un ralentissement de la demande aux États-Unis, ont renforcé les inquiétudes des investisseurs quant au redressement de Kering. Interrogée lors d'une conférence téléphonique sur la possibilité d'un retour à la croissance du groupe cette année, la directrice financière Armelle Poulou n'a pas souhaité commenter les perspectives, renvoyant à la publication des résultats annuels. Les certificats américains de dépôt (ADR) de Kering ont chuté de 11% après la publication de l'activité trimestrielle du groupe. Les ventes de Gucci, qui représentent environ la moitié du résultat opérationnel du groupe, se sont établies à 1,29 milliard d'euros au cours du trimestre. Sur l'ensemble du groupe, le chiffre d'affaires a reculé de 1% à données comparables. Selon Kering, la principale difficulté de Gucci reste la baisse de la fréquentation des magasins, particulièrement en Chine. Les ventes de la marque ont également légèrement reculé en Amérique du Nord. Pour attirer davantage de clients dans les magasins Gucci, Kering prévoit d'accroître ses investissements dans le marketing et l'expérience client, a déclaré Armelle Poulou. "Nous poursuivons l'exécution de notre plan avec la plus grande discipline", a déclaré Armelle Poulou. Elle a ajouté que le groupe avait déjà réduit son réseau de distribution de 105 magasins et anticipait désormais au moins 125 fermetures nettes sur l’exercice 2026. PRESSION SUR DEMNA Kering a nommé l'an dernier Luca de Meo pour restructurer le groupe. Après une hausse initiale à l'annonce de son arrivée, le titre Kering a perdu de son élan. L'action affiche un recul d'environ 8% sur un an, dans un contexte de repli plus général du secteur du luxe. Luca de Meo vise à doubler la marge opérationnelle de Kering d'ici à la fin de la décennie, à partir d'un niveau de 11,1% en 2025, grâce à des réductions de coûts, à de nouvelles fermetures de magasins et à une rationalisation de la chaîne d'approvisionnement. Des analystes estiment toutefois que ces seules mesures d'efficacité ne suffiront pas à relancer des marques qui ont perdu de leur attrait. Le directeur artistique de Saint Laurent, [USN:L8N45V0BG TEXT:"Anthony Vaccarello"], et [USN:FWN4611AW TEXT:"Sean McGirr"], d'Alexander McQueen, ont tous deux quitté leurs fonctions ce mois-ci. Les médias spécialisés spéculent également sur l'avenir de Pierpaolo Piccioli, directeur artistique de Balenciaga. Ces changements devraient accentuer encore la pression sur Demna, qui s'apprête à boucler sa première année complète à la tête de Gucci, qu'il a cherché à relancer en misant sur une esthétique audacieuse et sensuelle rappelant les succès de la marque sous Tom Ford. Demna a également adopté une approche inhabituelle en matière de production, en délocalisant en Chine la fabrication de ses premiers modèles de baskets.

item.title: Ahead of the US midterms, Gen Z investors are making portfolio changes
item.description: Brandon Gaw is monitoring the news to adjust investments that he thinks could be hit hard by pre-election volatility ahead of the US midterms.
item.dc:creator: Hani Richter
item.content:encoded: Brandon Gaw, an Oregon-based engineering student and investor. Courtesy Brandon Gaw/Handout via REUTERS Brandon Gaw, an Oregon-based engineering student and investor, isn't just watching the news to stay in the know. He's also monitoring it to adjust investments that he thinks could be hit hard by pre-election volatility ahead of the US midterms . “When others are fearful, that's the best time to invest,” he says. One issue the 22-year-old is watching closely is the prospect of tighter restrictions involving Chinese-made memory chips entering the US market, as well as increased competition. Against this backdrop, Gaw says he is holding more cash and selling shares in smaller and newer companies that are more dependent on investors' excitement about AI, which he believes could be especially vulnerable to election uncertainty. Every few weeks, Gaw trades stocks worth $5,000 to $10,000. “In my opinion, those are going to get hit the most,” he says. Brandon Gaw, an Oregon-based engineering student and investor. Courtesy Brandon Gaw/Handout via REUTERS Gaw accepts he’s taking more risk because of his age compared to an investor who may need their money sooner for retirement or a house. But he’s also investing in more established companies, including Microsoft, Google, Nvidia and Apple. “If anything, I added a few more positions in those companies,” he says. “I don't think they're going to run out of business anytime soon.” For now, Gaw’s portfolio is fairly spread out: crypto, gold and silver collectively account for about 5% to 10%; ETFs make up around 30%; and individual stocks account for 60%. He has not made changes to his retirement investments. Taking a long-term view, Gaw says a market dip does not matter much to him if the S&P 500 falls. “I think these pullbacks are pretty good buying opportunities,” he says. THE WIDER TREND Nearly three-quarters of Gen Z investors have changed their retirement savings or portfolios in anticipation of the midterm election outcomes, compared to just 17% of Baby Boomers, according to a recent Nationwide Retirement Institute survey of over 2,000 US investors. Tyler McConville, a Wisconsin-based certified financial planner and private wealth advisor at Capital Group, says “The challenge is determining which information actually matters to a long-term financial plan.” While it is important to pay attention to elections and policy changes, markets have historically been influenced more by economic fundamentals and specific policy outcomes. “The biggest risk is when investors make long-term portfolio decisions based on short-term political concerns,” he says. KEY TAKEAWAYS Don’t make speculative trades. Use market-moving events as a reminder to review your investments and to consider how elections could affect certain sectors. Keep diversification in mind. Gaw spreads his investments across individual stocks, ETFs, crypto and precious metals, while reducing his exposure to stocks that he considers volatile. A diversified portfolio can help limit reliance on any one investment or sector. Focus on economic fundamentals. Rather than assuming one political party will be good or bad for stocks, consider factors such as inflation, interest rates, corporate earnings and specific policy changes when assessing your investments. Have a money lesson or story to share? Tell us what worked for you — or what didn’t — by emailing hani.richter@tr.com .

item.title: Japan to arrange private investments worth $6.36 billion in Bangladesh, Nikkei reports
item.description: Japan will agree to arrange 1 trillion yen ($6.36 billion) in private-sector investments in Bangladesh over the next five years, the Nikkei newspaper reported on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Japan will agree to arrange 1 trillion yen ($6.36 billion) in private-sector investments in Bangladesh over the next five years, the Nikkei newspaper reported on Thursday. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will host her Bangladesh counterpart Tarique Rahman for a summit in Japan this month, and a joint statement will mention the arrangement, the report said. The investments are expected to go into automobile and other manufacturing industries, as well as the construction of energy facilities, Nikkei reported. It will also involve companies entering the Bangladesh Special Economic Zone being developed by parties including Japanese trading house Sumitomo Corp (8053.T) , the newspaper added. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. ($1 = 157.1900 yen)

item.title: Anthropic IPO stands alone as AI market jitters sideline others
item.description: A once-robust fall calendar for technology IPOs is down to just Anthropic.
item.dc:creator: Echo Wang
item.content:encoded: A once-robust fall calendar for technology IPOs is down to just Anthropic. The AI lab is pressing ahead to hold its initial public offering as planned in the middle of next month after making its prospectus public as early as late October, people familiar with the matter said, cautioning the plan and the dates are subject to change. Anthropic's planned IPO will test whether its position at the center of the booming AI business, which some investors believe to deem worthy of a potential $1.5 trillion valuation, can overcome a market environment that might typically prompt bankers and deal lawyers to counsel delay. Anthropic is expected to begin marketing its shares to prospective investors during the week of November 9, one of the people said. Other companies in the artificial intelligence infrastructure and data center sectors have delayed their listings, facing a rise in interest rates that has helped fuel a punishing selloff in shares and bonds of AI operators such as CoreWeave (CRWV.O) and broader questions about the sustainability of AI spending. The contrast underscores Anthropic's appeal to investors even as concerns about competition from open-source models and AI safety weigh on the sector. Many large investors remain bullish on Anthropic’s prospects despite the fall turbulence, viewing the firm as one of the few opportunities to gain exposure to a technology sector that long-term investors cannot afford to ignore. Other issuers are reluctant to compete with Anthropic for institutional investors' attention and capital, two of the people said. Anthropic declined to comment. VALUATIONS COMING UNDER PRESSURE The AI sector pullback follows a string of IPO delays and withdrawals since September, as market volatility and rising interest rates have made it harder for companies to secure attractive valuations. Switch, a data center operator, and Nscale, an AI infrastructure provider, have pushed their IPO plans back to later this year, people familiar with the matter said, while stressing that plans remain fluid and subject to change. Nscale’s delay was partly driven by the need to address comments from SEC staff, one other person said. SoftBank-backed SB Energy has also postponed its listing, Reuters previously reported. NScale declined to comment. Switch didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Blackstone-backed [USN:L6N45Z09R TEXT:"AirTrunk REIT"] and Nvidia (NVDA.O) -backed [USN:P8N42P0IJ TEXT:"Firmus"] have pulled or paused their offerings, Reuters has reported. Oura's recent IPO has added to the caution among prospective issuers. The offering attracted little participation from long-only investors, a person familiar with the matter said, raising concerns about the depth of demand from institutional investors that typically provide a stable base of shareholders for newly listed companies. SCRUTINY ON MULTIPLE FRONTS The retreat from AI infrastructure listings reflects growing scrutiny of the enormous capital required to build data centers and whether future demand will justify the investment. Recent developments involving CoreWeave have added to concerns about a potential slowdown in AI spending, although some market participants do not expect such a downturn to materialize. Nscale publicly filed its IPO registration statement in September, while Switch submitted its filing confidentially, Reuters reported previously. A confidential filing allows a company to work with regulators on its registration statement before disclosing financial and business details to the public. Companies typically publish the filing ahead of investor roadshows, when they begin marketing shares to prospective investors.

item.title: Will US Treasury scrap 20-year bond sales?
item.description: The US Treasury's auction of 20-year bonds on Wednesday won’t be the last, but this long-term debt instrument's days may be numbered.
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: The US Treasury's auction of 20-year bonds on Wednesday won’t be the last, but this long-term debt instrument's days may be numbered. Long-term borrowing costs are high. Yields on 10-year and 30-year Treasuries earlier this month rose to their highest levels since 2002, reaching 5.36% and 5.66%, respectively. The 5.469% that Treasury paid to borrow $13 billion on Wednesday was the highest yield at a 20-year auction since 1986. Discussion of whether the government should scrap this less liquid maturity altogether has intensified recently. Meanwhile, US federal debt has crossed the $40 trillion threshold, while Washington's interest bill for fiscal 2026 hit a record $1.36 trillion, putting interest payments as a share of GDP at a historic high of 3.2%. These metrics are all rising. When debt is above $40 trillion, a few basis points lower in borrowing costs can save billions. This points to an obvious strategy for lowering average government borrowing costs: lighten the load at the long end of the curve and borrow more at the front, where rates are lower. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent appears intent on doing just that. In August, Treasury announced it would at least double its $2 billion scheduled buybacks of longer-dated debt, referring to 10-year notes and 20- and 30-year bonds. It later increased that to $6 billion. Treasury said this reflected its "desire to provide greater liquidity support" to certain parts of the curve. That may be true, but it also just happens to align with longer-term efforts to shorten Treasury’s maturity profile. Around 22% of US public debt is currently in T-bills, which mature in one year or less, compared with around 15% five years ago. This is far from a “risk-free” strategy. By increasing the share of short-term debt, the government gives up the security of longer-term financing, meaning it must refinance more often. This "rollover risk" exposes the government to bouts of market shocks or volatility. But Bessent has few options. DEAR PRUDENCE A sudden burst of deficit-reduction fervor could sweep across Washington, leading to huge spending cuts or large tax hikes. But that's unlikely. The US budget deficit hit $2 trillion in fiscal 2026, more than 6% of GDP, and there is little appetite in the White House to tackle it. President Donald Trump recently pledged to mail $5,000 checks to every adult in the country if his Republican Party wins both houses of Congress in the midterm elections on November 3, a splurge that would cost over $1.1 trillion, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. Absent serious belt-tightening, Treasury has to consider other measures to help lower long-term borrowing costs. One could be reducing sales of the 20-year bond or getting rid of it entirely. The 20-year is one of the least liquid parts of the yield curve, with a limited supply of natural buyers. That means the government often has to offer a slightly more attractive yield. Markets will find out more in the first week of November when Treasury unveils its quarterly refunding plans. What can we expect? Normally, very little. In the words of the Treasury itself, the debt auction process, calendar and issuance amounts should be “regular and predictable” to ensure smooth functioning of the world's largest and most important market. But these are not normal times. The Treasury’s $6 billion accelerated buyback plan proved to be a bit of a flop, as the government failed to purchase the full amount in the first two rounds of buybacks in September. More importantly, long-dated yields rose as much as 50 basis points following the buyback announcement. Citi's US rates strategists expect 20-year and 30-year auction sizes to be reduced by $3 billion, with the gap filled by additional bill issuance. Treasury may also opt for more flexibility by keeping auction sizes unchanged but signaling that future adjustments are in play. Alternatively, Treasury may decide to retain the status quo. Analysts at JPMorgan reckon the scale of borrowing required in the coming years is so huge that it would "not be prudent" to discontinue a "critical" source of funding from an instrument that raises $168 billion a year. What's more, yields might be high, but they're not disconnected from current economic fundamentals, they argue. Given that the midterm elections are also in the first week of November, Treasury’s quarterly refunding plan may not be absolutely top of mind for investors. But that might be a mistake, as subtle changes in the government’s funding strategy could have big implications down the line. item.title: Ambani's heir Akash steps into the spotlight as India's Jio goes public
item.description: In Asia's richest family that controls the oil-to-retail Reliance empire, Mukesh Ambani's eldest son Akash is set to take centre stage as their telecoms and digital unit nears a stock market debut.
item.dc:creator: Vibhuti Sharma
item.content:encoded: In Asia's richest family that controls the oil-to-retail Reliance empire, Mukesh Ambani's eldest son Akash is set to take centre stage as their telecoms and digital unit nears a stock market debut. Akash Ambani, who turned 35 on Friday, is the managing director of Jio Platforms, whose $3.2 billion IPO this week was [USN:L4N46512K TEXT:"fully subscribed"] within two hours of opening for public bidding, a rare feat for an Indian offering of this size. Though Ambani senior still chairs the holding company Jio Platforms, Akash was anointed chairman of its money-spinning telecoms unit in 2022, in what was widely seen as part of the billionaire’s succession planning. In a sign of his growing clout, Akash led the pitch at Jio Platforms' IPO event last week where he briefed about the company's 533 million customers and profit margins. While his twin sister shared the stage, their father skipped the event. "I’m here as a representative of the entire company," he said. Industry executives who work with Akash described him as an extremely approachable executive who is very hands-on with technology. While Akash weighs in on "some of the bigger calls", he doesn't interfere in day-to-day business decisions. But he does deal with their most marquee investors including Meta, said one executive, who has worked closely on the IPO and with Akash. "He is the one who makes the calls to Mark Zuckerberg," the executive added. Meta is among Jio's largest shareholders with a near 10% stake. In 2020, it joined Google and other global investors in putting 1.52 trillion rupees into the company, worth $20.5 billion at the time. However, Akash and his father -- who are both night owls -- manage investor relationships separately, the industry executive said. Mukesh is closer to many sovereign wealth funds, while his son takes the position as Reliance's Silicon Valley man. Reliance and Meta did not respond to Reuters queries. CREATING THE RELIANCE BRAND Akash holds a bachelor’s in Economics from Brown University in the US and, as an avid sports enthusiast, plays a key role in the management of an Indian Premier League cricket franchise. Married in 2019, he has two children. By Thursday, the IPO’s retail portion was [USN:L1N46807C TEXT:"fully subscribed"], the employee quota drew bids for nearly twice the shares on offer and the existing Reliance shareholders quota was 2.58 times subscribed, exchange data showed. That interest from small investors is reminiscent of how Akash's grandfather Dhirubhai Ambani, who died in 2002, built Reliance's brand image with shareholders, holding large-scale meets in Mumbai’s open grounds in the 1980s that turned Reliance into a company that helps create long-term wealth. The conglomerate's Mumbai listed shares — that have a current market capitalization of $172 billion — have risen 330-fold since 1990. As Akash spoke at the event last week, a garlanded portrait of a smiling Dhirubhai was propped on an easel, while the screen showed black-and-white photos of old shareholder meets. JUST A TELCO? Jio's telecoms business was launched in 2016 and disrupted the market by offering free voice and data. Today, on the basis of customers in a single country, Jio's 500 million-plus users are second only to China Mobile (600941.SS) . Jio Platforms says Akash is leading its long-term "strategic roadmap to transform connectivity and digital services in India" from 4G to 5G and now AI. The company offers apps, digital services and home devices, but telecoms still brings in nearly 90% of its $15.45 billion revenue and around 94% of its profit. Akash and Jio appear keen to dispel the notion that Jio is just a telecoms company. The first line of the company overview in its prospectus reads: "We are a technology platform." Asked about rivalry with Bharti Airtel and Vodafone Idea, Akash told the Business Standard newspaper recently that "Jio is not just a telco," but a digital services company built on connectivity. At last week's event, he talked up plans to offer AI-powered call summaries and transcription in 12 Indian languages to Jio’s users, saying, "We’re the only play in town that can do that." "What we have is an innate understanding of our Jio customers," he said.

item.title: US banks are blocking third-party AI agents access to customer accounts, sources say
item.description: They are increasingly concerned sophisticated AI agents could harm the banking system.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Major US banks have been blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions, two people familiar with the situation said, following a report that AI agents were accessing bank accounts and taking actions independent of user instructions. The banking industry has become increasingly concerned that sophisticated AI agents could harm the banking system and the institutions trusted to hold people's wealth. An Axios report on Thursday said some AI agents attempted to take actions that appeared to be independent of user instructions, citing people familiar with the matter. In some cases, bank customers have shared their login ID and password with agents, with banks typically flagging and blocking those transactions, a person in the banking industry said. Still, such transactions cannot be deemed unauthorized if credentials were shared by the customer. Morgan Stanley (MS.N) has blocked third-party agents from accessing its platforms, but it had not seen any instances of unauthorized or rogue AI agents, according to a person familiar with the matter. Top banking executives earlier this month [USN:L4N45Z1M8 TEXT:"discussed the risks of AI agents"] acting on customers' behalf, with some warning the technology is adding significant risks for both customers and banks. JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) CEO Jamie Dimon earlier this month said the largest US lender was developing tools to navigate the risk of AI agents carrying out tasks on their own. "We're not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside the company because that's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," he said at the time. Charles Schwab (SCHW.N) CEO Richard Wurster earlier this month also said the brokerage was blocking unauthorized agents. "I get a report every day tracking how many times we've had to block one of the different agents, and it's not many because I think people aren't using it in that way in their financial life. We are blocking it because we want to have control over authentication and the experience," Wurster said.
